overview: This file documents U.S. diplomatic monitoring of Japan’s worsening financial position in early 1932, set against the abandonment of the gold standard and military operations in Manchuria and Shanghai. Alongside an extensive State Department index covering Japanese financial affairs from 1931 to 1938, it includes consular and embassy reporting on specie reserves, foreign balances and debts, yen depreciation, exchange and gold controls, budgetary measures, military appropriations, bond refinancing, and possible foreign loans. Correspondence involving Thomas W. Lamont and Representative Louis T. McFadden also reveals American financial and political resistance to lending that might sustain Japanese military expansion, while reports on Mitsui speculation, South Manchurian Railway financing, and British commercial anxieties connect monetary instability to business interests, imperial policy, and international competition.
interest: The file is especially useful for tracing how American officials and financiers understood the relationship between Japan’s monetary crisis and its military expansion at a pivotal moment in 1932. Its mixture of diplomatic reports, bankers’ assessments, congressional intervention, confidential correspondence, rumors of Mitsui speculation, and cross-references exposes the networks through which financial intelligence circulated. The lengthy retrospective index also makes the file valuable as a research guide to the broader State Department record on Japanese budgets, borrowing, exchange policy, gold movements, and war expenditure through 1938.
